subject: chemistry
question_text: Write the effect of temperature on surface tension and viscosity. Give the reason for it.

verification.note: Chapter 4 (States of Matter) is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.62-66), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. The book prints NO Long Answer section for this chapter, so no 8-mark form is invented. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The effect
lines: As the temperature of a liquid increases, BOTH
its surface tension and its viscosity decrease.
steps.why: Both properties are produced by intermolecular attractive forces, so they respond to temperature in the same direction — downward as the liquid gets hotter.
common_mistakes: Splitting the two: saying one increases and the other decreases. Both decrease.
Answering for a gas. Gas viscosity behaves differently; this question is about liquids.
steps.memory_tip: Hot liquids pour easily and spread easily: both viscosity and surface tension have dropped.
steps.margin_note: One clear sentence covering BOTH properties earns the mark.

steps.label: The reason
lines: Raising the temperature increases the kinetic
energy of the molecules, so the intermolecular

lines.text: Weaker effective attractions → lower surface tension and lower viscosity

steps.why: Surface tension comes from the inward pull on surface molecules, and viscosity from attractions between flowing layers. Faster-moving molecules overcome both attractions more easily, so both properties fall together.
common_mistakes: Saying the forces themselves disappear. The attractions remain; the faster motion makes them less effective.
Giving the effect again as the reason. The reason is the kinetic-energy argument.
steps.memory_tip: One cause, two effects: more kinetic energy makes the same attractions count for less, so both properties drop.
steps.margin_note: The chain KE up → attractions less effective → both down is the full reason.

insider_note: The word both is the trap — scripts that treat only surface tension, or only viscosity, are marked as half answers.
